scenes.narration:
When coding agents share a repository, writing code is only part of the job. Their changes also have to fit together. That's the problem NERUDO is built to handle.

This is the public application. This demo uses six scripted clients, using Git forks, submissions, checks, and receipts. They're scripted clients, rather than six live language models; we'll look at the model evidence later.

In the graph, you can follow work as it reaches main. Each agent has an isolated Artifacts fork, while one sequencer coordinates integration for the repository. It groups compatible changes, checks the resulting tree, and publishes a batch.

That gives agents something concrete to work with: a task, an attempt, preserved context, and a receipt that explains the outcome. You can still clone the repository with ordinary Git. Collaboration happens around that familiar repository, with a clear path from isolated work to shared main.

scenes.narration:
Repairing a dependency is one kind of coordination. Another is deciding between different answers to the same task. Here, three attempts are competing to solve one problem.

The Compare view brings those attempts together. Each is applied to current main and trial checked, without publishing it. You can compare the verdict, the paths it changes, and the diff, rather than judging only from the agent's description.

The plans sit alongside the code. They're pinned to the submitted revision, so a later edit to an agent's notes doesn't silently change what the reviewer is evaluating. That makes it possible to compare both the implementation and the reasoning that produced it.

A passing trial gives the person useful evidence for a choice. The selected attempt still goes through its own landing check, and the others close as not picked. This page is part of the scripted demo. Its purpose is to make alternatives reviewable before one of them becomes the shared result.

scenes.narration:
Choosing an implementation is also where human authority needs to stay clear. Repository rules decide which changes need a signature, including sensitive paths and changes to the rules themselves.

This approval is already recorded. We're viewing it anonymously, without performing a signing action. It applies to the exact submitted change and its governing rules, so it can't be carried over to a changed commit.

The release page shows the same principle at another boundary. The sequencer creates the annotated release tag only after the release statement has been signed. In the Signature tab, a reviewer can inspect who signed and which commit was released.

Those records also matter during recovery. If new rules have landed, they must become active before the next change is admitted, even after a crash. Independent verification can check the authority trail against the Git repository. That connects the approval you see here to the actual code, rather than leaving it as an interface status alone.

scenes.narration:
So far, we've been looking at scripted product behavior. Here are the records from actual coding clients. On October thirteenth, Claude, Codex, and Hermes overlapped on an isolated Worker build. Claude and Codex completed and landed. Hermes timed out after nine hundred seconds, before submitting its change.

The coordination trace shows a useful detail: Claude changed the currency API, and Codex's first revision failed integrated CI. Codex read Claude's pinned context, repaired its caller, and landed revision two. Claude also completed native planner and reviewer children.

Verification and eleven external runtime tests passed, but full fixture acceptance failed because the receipt feature was missing. That's the initial two-of-three result preserved in this record.

The workflow document also preserves earlier successful three-client runs. A later, separate Hermes recovery landed the missing feature and passed external acceptance, but its parent client still timed out. There are three eventual landings, while the original concurrent attempt still has only two completed workflows.

scenes.narration:
These benchmarks ask a different question: how quickly can the integration service land prepared changes across many repositories? They measure integration, separately from the time a model spends producing code.

On one thousand repositories, the five-minute run measured about nine hundred ninety-four landings per second in its measured window. Two hundred ninety-nine thousand nine hundred eighty-eight of three hundred thousand changes landed; twelve pushes failed. The workload used synthetic, disjoint changes with no CI, so that rate describes those conditions.

The breadth experiment spread work across ten thousand quiet repositories, at about five hundred aggregate landings per second. Each synthetic agent submitted one change every twenty seconds. That's useful evidence about repository breadth, but it isn't ten thousand language models coding simultaneously.

The highest measured rate was one thousand nine hundred seventy-eight landings per second across two thousand repositories, during a healthy ninety-second window. That run stopped during Artifacts failures at one hundred thirty-one seconds. The failure stays in the report, alongside the peak. It's a short measured window, not sustained capacity or a promise about a conflicting workload with checks enabled.

scenes.narration:
Repository count is one dimension; repository size is another. The large-repository experiment here landed a seven hundred twenty-eight megabyte tip, then passed read-back and Git object verification. The reported fourteen megabyte peak is WASM linear memory. It doesn't measure all isolate memory or demonstrate arbitrary monorepo CI.

The component view explains how the pieces fit. Workers host the application and the Rust WASM sequencer. A Durable Object coordinates each repository, while Artifacts supplies Git storage and isolated agent forks. A service binding connects integration to a separate CI Worker.

That arrangement spreads independent repositories across the platform, while keeping one serialized integration authority inside each repository. Batching makes compatible work share a check. Local fault regressions then exercise what happens when a process crashes, approval rules change, or allowance accounting is replayed. The source makes those recovery contracts inspectable, alongside the measurements you've just seen.

scenes.narration:

Start with the workspace tests and the local fault harness. For a live deployment, use your own credentials and an isolated namespace, following the three-Worker instructions. That keeps reproduction separate from the public demo.

The cost section makes another distinction. Artifacts billing begins on October fourteenth. Historical campaign spending excluded the then-free Artifacts service; paid projections also need repository storage, retries, checks, and model inference. They are estimates, not observed production invoices.

There's still work ahead on sustained conflicting workloads, broader runtime CI, and production service guarantees. What you can inspect today is a working collaboration contract: isolated attempts, integrated checks, useful receipts, preserved intent, and signatures tied to exact code. NERUDO is open source under MIT or Apache two point zero.

The large-repository experiment here landed a seven hundred twenty-eight megabyte tip, then passed read-back and Git object verification. The reported fourteen megabyte peak is WASM linear memory. It doesn't measure all isolate memory or demonstrate arbitrary monorepo CI.

The component view explains how the pieces fit. Workers host the application and the Rust WASM sequencer. A Durable Object coordinates each repository, while Artifacts supplies Git storage and isolated agent forks. A service binding connects integration to a separate CI Worker.

That arrangement spreads independent repositories across the platform, while keeping one serialized integration authority inside each repository. Batching makes compatible work share a check. Local fault regressions then exercise what happens when a process crashes, approval rules change, or allowance accounting is replayed. The source makes those recovery contracts inspectable, alongside the measurements you've just seen.

scenes.title: 01 / A Git platform for concurrent coding agents
scenes.label: Public product · scripted six-client demo
scenes.narration: NERUDO is a Git platform built around concurrent coding agents. This is the public application, and this repository is a scripted six-client product demonstration. The clients exercise real Git forks, submissions, checks, and receipts; they are not six live language models. Each agent works in an isolated Artifacts fork. A Durable Object provides one authoritative integration path for this repository. Instead of every agent racing to update main, the sequencer groups compatible changes, checks the integrated tree, and publishes a batch. The graph records what landed and how. Tasks, attempts, preserved context, and actionable receipts form the collaboration contract. The familiar Git repository remains available to ordinary clones and tools.

scenes.title: 02 / The integrated check catches a stale caller
scenes.label: Recorded demo outcome · actual CI receipt
scenes.narration: The hard case is a shared API changing while another agent is still using its old shape. A change can pass on its own base and fail after integration. Here the receipt preserves the rejected revision and the diagnostic from the integrated TypeScript check. The agent can fetch the new main, read the relevant context, repair its caller, and resubmit the same logical change as a new revision. This is real checking of the integrated batch tip. It is important to state the guarantee precisely: a passing batch tip does not prove that every intermediate commit in that batch is independently buildable. The revision history lets a reviewer inspect the rejection and subsequent repair, rather than losing the reason for the retry.

scenes.title: 03 / Compare competing attempts and their plans
scenes.label: Scripted demo · trials do not publish a winner
scenes.narration: An agent-first platform also needs a way to compare alternative solutions. This task has competing attempts. Each attempt is applied to current main and trial checked without publishing it. The view puts verdicts, changed paths, plans, and diffs side by side. A passing trial is evidence for a choice, not permission to merge every competing implementation. The person can pick an attempt; that attempt still gets its own landing check, and the others close as not picked. The plan is preserved with the exact submitted revision, so the reviewer can understand the intent behind the code. These plans came from the scripted demonstration. The next evidence chapter separately identifies work performed by actual coding-model clients.

scenes.title: 04 / Human authority stays bound to exact commits
scenes.label: Recorded approval and release · anonymous read-only view
scenes.narration: Autonomy needs clear governance boundaries. Repository rules determine which changes need a human signature, including sensitive paths and changes to the rules themselves. The approval shown here was already recorded; this anonymous walkthrough performs no signing action. The signature is tied to the exact change and governing rules. Recovery must activate newly landed rules before admitting the next change, including after a crash. A release is another explicit boundary. The sequencer creates the annotated tag only after the release statement is signed. The signature view exposes who signed and what commit was released. Verification can run from outside the service against the released repository, so the authority record is not confined to a screenshot of the interface.

scenes.title: 05 / Real coding models, including unfinished outcomes
scenes.label: Fresh isolated run · pinned build 79c259ad · 2/3 complete · acceptance incomplete
scenes.narration: This evidence records real native coding-model workflows. The fresh October thirteenth attempt ran Claude, Codex, and Hermes concurrently on an earlier isolated Worker build. Claude and Codex landed; Hermes reached the nine-hundred-second timeout. Two of three workflows completed. Codex’s first revision failed after Claude changed the currency API. It read Claude’s pinned context and landed a repaired second revision. External verification and eleven runtime tests passed, but full acceptance failed because the receipt feature was missing. Claude’s native planner and reviewer children completed. The first attempt is immutable; any Hermes recovery is separate. Dated October twelfth records also show successful three-client workflows, with three verified landings in three batches. These small experiments demonstrate interoperability, not large-scale model concurrency.

scenes.title: 06 / Scale measurements with the conditions visible
scenes.label: Recorded synthetic benchmarks · scope and failures included
scenes.narration: The scale evidence measures integration, separately from model generation. On one thousand repositories, a five-minute run recorded about nine hundred ninety-four landings per second in the measured window. Two hundred ninety-nine thousand nine hundred eighty-eight of three hundred thousand changes landed, with twelve push failures. The changes were synthetic and disjoint, with no CI. A separate breadth run exercised ten thousand quiet repositories at about five hundred aggregate landings per second. Each synthetic agent submitted one change every twenty seconds. The peak result was one thousand nine hundred seventy-eight per second across two thousand repositories during a healthy ninety-second window. That run stopped during Artifacts failures at one hundred thirty-one seconds. The peak is not a five-minute capacity claim. These conditions and failures are part of the result.

scenes.title: 07 / Cloudflare architecture and verification bounds
scenes.label: Workers · Durable Objects · Artifacts · isolated CI Worker
scenes.narration: The implementation uses Workers for the app and Rust W A S M sequencer, Durable Objects for repository coordination, Artifacts for Git storage and isolated forks, and a service-bound CI Worker. Scale comes from independent repositories and batching within each repository; one repository still has a serialized integration authority. A large-repository experiment landed a seven hundred twenty-eight megabyte tip and passed read-back and Git object verification. Its reported fourteen megabyte peak measures W A S M linear memory, not total isolate RAM or arbitrary monorepo CI. Local fault regressions exercise crash recovery, approval rules, and allowance accounting. The source and run instructions let a reviewer reproduce those checks in an isolated environment and inspect the contracts behind the product.

scenes.title: 08 / Reproduce the work and see what remains
scenes.label: Public source · MIT OR Apache-2.0 · reproducible evidence
scenes.narration: The repository includes the CLI, fixtures, deployment instructions, fault harness, benchmark drivers, and recorded evidence. Clone the public source, run the workspace tests and W A S M check, then use an isolated namespace for live reproduction. The cost discussion separates historical campaign spending from paid Artifacts operations and storage, CI, and model inference. This submission has not demonstrated one hundred thousand simultaneous coding agents on one repository, sustained conflicting workloads with general runtime CI, or a production service-level agreement. Its contribution is a working agent collaboration contract: isolated work, integrated checks, useful receipts, preserved intent, competing attempts, and exact human authority. The public application and source make that design concrete and reviewable.
